e-21707.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
e-21707.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-7x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Find the general solution to the system of ODEs above.

*Hint: ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/5388e1d5a2d29c3930b904d418b3a69615683bff1278d45a202d8405b150cede.png) where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/85fc07cc4bce6e748a6b0184a3fc0a1ef75bf37e29d68ea45cbbb94892d5b58d.png)*
e-21707.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/7f047425e15df4bb6bd8284f0e6267227ba31f6a251ceb45e040e6a508b519d6.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/2dff913b6a0163c9dff6e28d81690472f043de69e4796dffb58b16b933165450.png) So, the matrix of the system is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/c31b507ed2dac736cf47cbee9a967be4f4dc7deda44776e27a62be953834905b.png)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/716aafac0120d14538c3cb2cea689450e9655f0d94147b04c0903c3bb5cde753.png)

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-7t} & t{e}^{-7t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-7t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-7t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{-7t} \\ {e}^{-7t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-7t},\end{aligned}
$$

where $c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.$

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \, \mathbf{x}(0),
$$

where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{x}(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ of the system is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/dad0a2186f78aae6569b2d880e29a570f44b289a2fd1d804e989a3356b7f0074.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/bf7bc97a737f653b03369fa91a29f564703abf6172aba7ba6db62acae12c1af4.png) where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/d63e1f20fcf33dd0ba20d1ba2be8ae008888e794c0054da8b8628f182c501068.png)*
e-21723.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/cdd98c904dce4f0beebc1333ce00f3f54551a93eddb5a8e52af6392946c2f910.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/2dff913b6a0163c9dff6e28d81690472f043de69e4796dffb58b16b933165450.png) So, the matrix of the system is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/b6e79ba4308d37fec08efa34e15e009e938fc6df4bceba677837897c21602397.png)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi(t) \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \Phi_0(t) \mathbf{c} =e^{At} \, \mathbf{c},
$$

where $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t = t_0,$ we have 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0) = e^{At_0} \, \mathbf{c},
$$

and since $e^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
\mathbf{c} = e^{-At_0} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $\mathbf{x}(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(7(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(7(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-21711.knowledge_point: Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution: Homogeneous Systems
e-21711.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
\Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \qquad \Phi_0(0) = I_n.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ passing through $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ is presented below. 

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}$  

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,\mathbf{c}$ for some constant vector $\mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At}\,\mathbf{c}$ 

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t_0)=e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $(e^{A t_0})^{-1} \mathbf{x}(t_0)=(e^{At_0})^{-1} e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c}$  

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{c} = e^{-A t_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} e^{-At_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L8}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At - At_0} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

$\textrm{L9}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{A(t-t_0)} \mathbf{x}(t_0) \,$  

Fill in the blanks to justify each step of the following reasoning.

$\qquad$ Line $\textrm{L5}$ follows from $\textrm{L4}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/49f634e53afe213a0c192e6ef60e8499801a86a8d6a87d1776fafa62cef3192f.png)

$\qquad$ The property of the matrix exponential used in $\textrm{L8}$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/8b875a680318b797dc6b78d1c73b0012ede83a412435efafaf3064321fc406ee.png)

$\qquad$ Line $\textrm{L9}$ follows from $\textrm{L8}$ by the fact that  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/e576e779eada3b3a299cf45e14a1d6fbdfca5aa852bf2eb7eea70bdb22e0f41d.png)
e-21711.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\textrm{L4}$ and $\textrm{L5}.$ Starting from $\textrm{L4},$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t_0)=e^{A t_0} \, \mathbf{c},
$$

we multiply both sides on the left by $(e^{At_0})^{-1}$ to get

$$
(e^{A t_0})^{-1}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=(e^{At_0})^{-1}e^{A t_0}\,\mathbf{c},
$$

which is line $\textrm{L5}.$ Therefore, $\textrm{L5}$ follows from $\textrm{L4}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/22142a26bf70dc1ee58e7d7643acdad468ddfd7c9dc48c816f136afcae4d1320.png)

- Next, we justify the step $\textrm{L7}$ to $\textrm{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-At_0$ commute, we may combine exponentials:

$$
e^{At}e^{-At_0}=e^{At-At_0}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\textrm{L7}$ produces line $\textrm{L8}.$ Hence, the property of the matrix exponential used in $\textrm{L8}$ is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071035/assets/bab6ad7c1621beb36d016e72f1e040206b9bf70a2e21ff266ba5b71495a23ae2.png)

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L8}$ and $\textrm{L9}.$ Starting from $\textrm{L8},$

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{At-At_0}\mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

we rewrite the exponent using the algebraic identity $At-At_0=A(t-t_0)$ to get

$$
\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0),
$$

which is line $\textrm{L9}.$ Thus, $\textrm{L9}$ follows from $\textrm{L8}$ by the fact that $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt lightgray]{At-At_0=A(t-t_0)\text{ for any }t\text{ and }t_0}.$

Question 1
?

{x′(t)=3y(t)y′(t)=3x(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)], where A=[0330].

a
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]e3t+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
b
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]+c2[−sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
c
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]e−3t+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
d
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
e
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]e−3t
Submit

decision.explanation: The general solution is the given matrix exponential multiplied by an arbitrary constant vector: x(t)=e^{At}c. Expanding this product gives option d. Its two columns satisfy the system and are linearly independent because their determinant is cosh²(3t)−sinh²(3t)=1.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 1

{x′(t)=3y(t)y′(t)=3x(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)], where A=[0330].

a
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]e3t+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
b
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]+c2[−sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
c
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]e−3t+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
d
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]
e
x(t)=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)]e−3t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0330]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0330].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)][c1c2]=c1[cosh⁡(3t)sinh⁡(3t)]+c2[sinh⁡(3t)cosh⁡(3t)],

where c1,c2∈R.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(3t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 2

{x′(t)=−4y(t)y′(t)=4x(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[cos⁡(4t)−sin⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)], where A=[0−440].

a
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]+c2[−sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]e−4t
b
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]e4t+c2[−sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]
c
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]+c2[−sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]e4t
d
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]+c2[−sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]
e
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]+c2[sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]
Submit

decision.explanation: Multiplying the given matrix exponential by the arbitrary constant vector (c₁,c₂) gives option d. Both columns satisfy the system, and their determinant is cos²(4t)+sin²(4t)=1, so they form a fundamental matrix and give the general solution.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Hint: eAt=[cos⁡(4t)−sin⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)], where A=[0−440].

a

c

d
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]+c2[−sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]
e
x(t)=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]+c2[sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[0−440]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[0−440].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[cos⁡(4t)−sin⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[cos⁡(4t)−sin⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)][c1c2]=c1[cos⁡(4t)sin⁡(4t)]+c2[−sin⁡(4t)cos⁡(4t)],

where c1,c2∈R.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d: multiplying e^{At} by (c₁,c₂) gives exactly its two terms. Direct differentiation verifies both ODEs, and the column determinant is 1, so this is the general solution. Option c's extra e^{4t} introduces an additional derivative term and fails the system.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 3

{x′(t)=6x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=6y(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[e6tte6t0e6t], where A=[6106].

a
x(t)=c1[10]et+c2[t1]e6t
b
x(t)=c1[10]e6t+c2[11]e6t
c
x(t)=c1[10]e6t+c2[t1]e6t
d
x(t)=c1[10]e6t+c2[t1]e−6t
e

decision.explanation: Multiplying the given e^{At} by (c₁,c₂) gives x(t)=(c₁+c₂t)e^{6t} and y(t)=c₂e^{6t}, exactly option c. Differentiating verifies x′=6x+y and y′=6y; the arbitrary constants cover every initial condition.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{6t} \\ {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 3
?

{x′(t)=6x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=6y(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[e6tte6t0e6t], where A=[6106].

a
x(t)=c1[10]et+c2[t1]e6t
b
x(t)=c1[10]e6t+c2[11]e6t
c
x(t)=c1[10]e6t+c2[t1]e6t
d
x(t)=c1[10]e6t+c2[t1]e−6t
e
x(t)=c1[10]e6t+c2[11]e−6t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[6106]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[6106].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[e6tte6t0e6t].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[e6tte6t0e6t][c1c2]=c1[e6t0]+c2[te6te6t]=c1[10]e6t+c2[t1]e6t,

where c1,c2∈R.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{6t} \\ {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

history.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{6t} \\ {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 4
?

{x′(t)=2x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=2y(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[e2tte2t0e2t], where A=[2102].

a
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[t1]e2t
b
x(t)=c1[10]et+c2[11]e2t
c
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[11]e−2t
d
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[11]e2t
e
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[t1]e−2t
Submit

decision.explanation: The general solution is e^{At}(c₁,c₂), giving x(t)=(c₁+c₂t)e^{2t} and y(t)=c₂e^{2t}. This is option a; differentiation verifies both equations, and the constants allow every initial condition.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

{x′(t)=2x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=2y(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[e2tte2t0e2t], where A=[2102].

a
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[t1]e2t
b
x(t)=c1[10]et+c2[11]e2t
c
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[11]e−2t
d
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[11]e2t
e
x(t)=c1[10]e2t+c2[t1]e−2t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[2102]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[2102].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[e2tte2t0e2t].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[e2tte2t0e2t][c1c2]=c1[e2t0]+c2[te2te2t]=c1[10]e2t+c2[t1]e2t,

where c1,c2∈R.

verification.explanation: The revealed worked solution confirms option a. It gives x(t)=(c₁+c₂t)e^{2t} and y(t)=c₂e^{2t}, which satisfy x′=2x+y and y′=2y and allow arbitrary initial values. The deliberately submitted option b does not satisfy the system for arbitrary constants.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{2t} \\ {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

{x′(t)=−5x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=−5y(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[e−5tte−5t0e−5t], where A=[−510−5].

a
x(t)=c1[10]e−5t+c2[t1]e−5t
b
x(t)=c1[10]e−t+c2[t1]e−5t
c
x(t)=c1[10]e−5t+c2[11]e5t
d
x(t)=c1[10]e5t+c2[t1]e−5t
e

decision.explanation: Multiplying the given matrix exponential by (c₁,c₂) gives x(t)=(c₁+c₂t)e^{-5t} and y(t)=c₂e^{-5t}, exactly option a. Differentiation verifies both ODEs, and the arbitrary constants cover every initial condition.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{-5t} \\ {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-5t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-5t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Question 5
?

{x′(t)=−5x(t)+y(t)y′(t)=−5y(t) Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

Hint: eAt=[e−5tte−5t0e−5t], where A=[−510−5].

a
x(t)=c1[10]e−5t+c2[t1]e−5t
b
x(t)=c1[10]e−t+c2[t1]e−5t
c
x(t)=c1[10]e−5t+c2[11]e5t
d
x(t)=c1[10]e5t+c2[t1]e−5t
e
x(t)=c1[10]e−5t+c2[11]e−5t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we get x′(t)=[−510−5]x(t), where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)]. So, the matrix of the system is A=[−510−5].

Given the system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as x(t)=Φ(t)c, where Φ(t) is a fundamental matrix of the system, and c is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) of the system is given by Φ0(t)=eAt=[e−5tte−5t0e−5t].

Therefore, the general solution is

x(t)=Φ0(t)c=eAtc=[e−5tte−5t0e−5t][c1c2]=c1[e−5t0]+c2[te−5te−5t]=c1[10]e−5t+c2[t1]e−5t,

where c1,c2∈R.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the General Solution of a Homogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the general solution to the system of ODEs above?

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c \\  & ={e}^{At}\,c \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t{e}^{-5t} \\ {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-5t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}t \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-5t},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.$

Hint: eAt=[e−5tte−5t0e−5t], where A=[−510−5].

decision.explanation: Multiplying e^{At} by the initial vector (0,−3) gives x(t)=−3te^{-5t} and y(t)=−3e^{-5t}, which is option c. These satisfy both differential equations and the initial conditions x(0)=0, y(0)=−3.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3t{e}^{-5t} \\ -3{e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Φ0(t)=eAt=[e−5tte−5t0e−5t].

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 1 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-5t} & t{e}^{-5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3t{e}^{-5t} \\ -3{e}^{-5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{6t} \\ -4{e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=6x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t} & t{e}^{6t} \\ 0 & {e}^{6t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4t{e}^{6t} \\ -4{e}^{6t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{-3t} \\ 2{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-3x(t)+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,x(0),
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system, and $x(0)$ is the initial condition vector.

Now, using the given information, the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ of the system is given by

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & t{e}^{-3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{-3t} \\ 2{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

{x′(t)=2y(t)y′(t)=2x(t),[x(−2)y(−2)]=[0−2] Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)sinh⁡(2t)cosh⁡(2t)], where A=[0220].

a
[−2sinh⁡(2(t+2))−2cosh⁡(2(t+2))]
b
[2sinh⁡(2(t+2))2cosh⁡(2(t+2))]
c
[sinh⁡(2(t+2))cosh⁡(2(t+2))]
d
[−2cosh⁡(2(t+2))−2sinh⁡(2(t+2))]
e
[2cosh⁡(2(t+2))−2sinh⁡(2(t+2))]
Submit

decision.explanation: With initial time −2, the solution is e^{A(t+2)}(0,−2). Multiplication gives option a. At t=−2 it equals (0,−2), and differentiation verifies x′=2y and y′=2x.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(-2) \\ y(-2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have 

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-(-2))}\,x(-2) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t+2)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t+2)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t+2)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t+2))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t+2)) \\ -2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t+2))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=2x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(-2) \\ y(-2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$

Hint: eAt=[cosh⁡(4t)−sinh⁡(4t)−sinh⁡(4t)cosh⁡(4t)], where A=[0−4−40].

decision.explanation: The solution is e^{A(t−1)}(0,−2), giving x(t)=2sinh(4(t−1)) and y(t)=−2cosh(4(t−1)). This is option b. At t=1 the values are (0,−2), and differentiation verifies x′=−4y and y′=−4x.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(1) \\ y(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Homogeneous Initial Value Problem Using a Given Matrix Exponential: Shifted Initial Conditions
content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-4x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(1) \\ y(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$*
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the general solution of the system can be written as

$$
x(t)=Φ(t)\,c,
$$

where $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix of the system, and $c$ is a constant vector.

So, we can write our general solution as

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)c={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

where ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is the standard fundamental matrix of the system. Substituting $t={t}_{0},$ we have

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

and since ${e}^{At}$ is invertible for all $t,$ we have

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}).
$$

Plugging the above back into our expression for $x(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}\,{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}\,x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1)) & -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(4(t-1)) \\ -2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(4(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 16
?
Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In.

A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(t)=eAtc

L4: x(t0)=eAt0c

L5: (eAt0)−1x(t0)=(eAt0)−1eAt0c

L6: c=e−At0x(t0)

L7: x(t)=eAte−At0x(t0)

L8: x(t)=eAt−At0x(t0)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L4 follows from L3
 
by substituting t=t0
by substitution from line L2
using the fact that Φ0(0)=In
.

Line L6 follows from L5 by the fact that
 
(eAt0)−1eAt0=eAt0I
(eAt0)−1=e−At0
eAt0e−At0=Ie−At0
.

Line L8 follows from L7 by the fact that
 
eAte−At0=eA(t−t0)
eAt0=eAt for any matrix A
eXeY=eX+Y when X and Y commute
.
Submit

decision.explanation: L4 evaluates L3 at t=t₀. L6 uses (e^{At₀})⁻¹=e^{−At₀} and cancels the inverse product to I. L8 combines exponentials because At and −At₀ are scalar multiples of A and therefore commute. Field 3 option 0 is also a valid equivalent identity; option 2 directly states the property used in L8.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$  Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$

A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L3 and L4. Starting from L3, x(t)=eAtc, we evaluate both sides at t=t0 to obtain x(t0)=eAt0c which is line L4. Therefore, L4 follows from L3 by substituting t=t0.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Line L5 gives (eAt0)−1x(t0)=(eAt0)−1eAt0c. Since (eAt0)−1eAt0=In, the right-hand side simplifies to c, so c=(eAt0)−1x(t0). Simplify once, then apply (eAt0)−1=e−At0, to obtain c=e−At0x(t0), which is line L6. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by the fact that (eAt0)−1=e−At0.

  • Finally, we consider lines L7 and L8. Since At and −At0 commute, we can use the property eAte−At0=eAt−At0. Substituting this into line L7, we get line L8: x(t)=eAte−At0x(t0)=eAt−At0x(t0) Therefore, L8 follows from L7 by the fact that eXeY=eX+Y when X and Y commute.

Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$  

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$  

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that {{field-2}}.

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Line $\text{L5}$ gives

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c.
$$

Since $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}={I}_{n}$, the right-hand side simplifies to $c$, so

$$
c=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0}).
$$

Simplify once, then apply $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}$, to obtain

$$
c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L6}.$ Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by the fact that $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$

before.name: Question 17
before.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by {{field-3}}.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Starting from $\text{L4},$

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

we multiply both sides on the left by $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}$ to get

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides on the left by }({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L7}.$ Using line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

From line $\text{L6}$, we know that $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}).$ Substituting this expression for $c$ into the formula for $x(t)$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$

Question 17
?
Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In.

A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(t)=eAtc

L4: x(t0)=eAt0c

L5: (eAt0)−1x(t0)=(eAt0)−1eAt0c

L6: c=e−At0x(t0)

L7: x(t)=eAte−At0x(t0)

L8: x(t)=eAt−At0x(t0)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L5 follows from L4 by
using the identity (eAt0)−1=e−At0
integrating x(t)
using the identity (eAt0)−1=e−At0
multiplying both sides on the left by (eAt0)−1
.

Line L7 can be obtained by
substituting c=e−At0x(t0) into x(t)=eAtc
left-multiplying x(t)=eAtc by e−At
evaluating x(t)=eAtc at t=t0 and solving for c
substituting c=e−At0x(t0) into x(t)=eAtc
.

Line L8 follows from L7 by
the fact that eXeY=eX+Y when X and Y commute
the fact that (eAt0)−1=e−At0
the identity eXeY=eXY for matrices
the fact that eXeY=eX+Y when X and Y commute
.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L4 and L5. Starting from L4, x(t0)=eAt0c, we multiply both sides on the left by (eAt0)−1 to get (eAt0)−1x(t0)=(eAt0)−1eAt0c, which is line L5. Therefore, L5 follows from L4 by multiplying both sides on the left by (eAt0)−1.

  • Next, we consider line L7. Using line L3 we have x(t)=eAtc. From line L6, we know that c=e−At0x(t0). Substituting this expression for c into the formula for x(t) gives x(t)=eAte−At0x(t0), which is line L7. Thus, line L7 can be obtained by substituting c=e−At0x(t0) into x(t)=eAtc.

content.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Starting from $\text{L4},$

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

we multiply both sides on the left by $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}$ to get

$$
({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c,
$$

which is line $\text{L5}.$ Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides on the left by }({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}.$

- Next, we consider line $\text{L7}.$ Using line $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c.
$$

From line $\text{L6}$, we know that $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}).$ Substituting this expression for $c$ into the formula for $x(t)$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}),
$$

which is line $\text{L7}.$ Thus, line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by $\text{substituting }c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\text{ into }x(t)={e}^{At}c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ is true by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, every solution of the system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c\,\text{for some constant vector }c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ is true by $\text{the properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

content.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ is true by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that {{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ is a fundamental matrix for the system, every solution of the system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c\,\text{for some constant vector }c.
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ is true by $\text{the properties of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Starting from $\text{L3},$

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,c,
$$

we evaluate both sides at $t={t}_{0}$ to obtain

$$
x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c
$$

which is line $\text{L4}.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ $\text{by substituting }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Since $At$ and $-A{t}_{0}$ commute, we can use the property 

$$
{e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}.
$$

Substituting this into line $\text{L7},$ we get line $\text{L8}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0}) \\  & ={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by the fact that ${e}^{X}{e}^{Y}={e}^{X+Y}\text{ when }X\text{ and }Y\text{ commute}.$

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by  {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by substitution from lines {{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from $\text{L2},$ we have the identity

$$
x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c.
$$

Evaluating this identity at $t=0$ gives

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L3}.$ Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ From $\text{L3}$ we have

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

and from $\text{L4}$ we know ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.$ Substituting ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$ into $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c$ gives

$$
x(0)={I}_{n}c=c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L5}.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by $\text{substituting }{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}\text{ into }x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$, $\text{L2},$ $\text{L5},$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L1}$ we have ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At},$ and from $\text{L5}$ we know $c=x(0).$ Substituting ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$ from $\text{L1}$ and $c=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$ into $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ (line $\text{L2}$), we obtain

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0).
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ and substitution from $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L5}.$

Consider the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), where A is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix Φ0(t) is the unique solution to the initial value problem Φ0′(t)=AΦ0(t),Φ0(0)=In. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(0) is presented below.

L1: Let Φ0(t)=eAt

L2: x(t)=Φ0(t)c for some constant vector c

L3: x(0)=Φ0(0)c

L4: Φ0(0)=In

L5: x(0)=c

L6: x(t)=eAtx(0)

EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L2 and L3. Starting from L2, we have the identity x(t)=Φ0(t)c. Evaluating this identity at t=0 gives x(0)=Φ0(0)c, which is exactly line L3. Therefore, L3 follows from L2 by evaluating both sides at t=0.

  • Next, we consider lines L3, L4, and L5. From L3 we have x(0)=Φ0(0)c, and from L4 we know Φ0(0)=In. Substituting Φ0(0)=In into x(0)=Φ0(0)c gives x(0)=Inc=c, which is exactly line L5. Thus, L5 follows from lines L3 and L4 by substituting Φ0(0)=In into x(0)=Φ0(0)c.

  • Finally, we consider lines L1, L2, L5, and L6. From L1 we have Φ0(t)=eAt, and from L5 we know c=x(0). Substituting Φ0(t)=eAt from L1 and c=x(0) from L5 into x(t)=Φ0(t)c (line L2), we obtain x(t)=eAtx(0). Thus, L6 follows from L2 and substitution from L1 and L5.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms these selections: L3 evaluates L2 at t=0; L5 substitutes Φ₀(0)=Iₙ and uses Iₙc=c; L6 substitutes Φ₀(t)=e^{At} from L1 and c=x(0) from L5 into L2. Diagonalization does not justify L3.

content.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)\,c$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(0)=c$  

$\text{L6}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,x(0)$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}$ by  {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by substitution from lines {{field-3}}.

$$
x(0)={Φ}_{0}(0)c,
$$

which is exactly line $\text{L3}.$ Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{evaluating both sides at }t=0.$

$$

before.name: Question 20
before.problem:
Consider the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. You're given that the standard fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ is the unique solution to the initial value problem

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n}.
$$

A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}$

$\text{L2}:\,$ $x(t)={Φ}_{0}(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}\,c$ 

$\text{L4}:\,$ $x({t}_{0})={e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}x({t}_{0})=({e}^{A{t}_{0}})^{-1}{e}^{A{t}_{0}}\,c$

$\text{L6}:\,$ $c={e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}{e}^{-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L8}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At-A{t}_{0}}x({t}_{0})\,$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})\,$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ can be obtained by {{field-2}}.
